## My Reasoning

I've farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. The North China Plain has one logic: winter wheat, then summer maize on the same ground. I've done this rotation for forty years and I won't change it now. The soil knows it, I know it, and the markets know it.

I have about 10 mu of arable land I manage myself. My children are in Shijiazhuang — I hire a machine contractor for sowing and harvest, which costs money but saves my back and time at 65.

**Wheat (winter):** I'll use the Kenong 199 variety — it's well-adapted to Quzhou's soil, resistant to lodging, and the county extension station has been promoting it. Not traditional seed, not hybrid — it's an improved open-pollinated variety that's become standard here. I'll do a deep plough before sowing in October to break the hardpan and incorporate the maize stalks. I'll irrigate three times: once before winter sets in, once at jointing in late March, once at heading in late April. That third irrigation is the one I'm always tempted to skip to save water costs, but I've seen yields drop 40–50 kg/mu when I do. I won't skip it. Three pesticide applications: one seed treatment, one for aphids and powdery mildew around jointing, one for fusarium head blight at heading. I use a drone service now — far more even coverage than the knapsack sprayer I used for decades.

**Maize (summer):** I'll direct-seed hybrid maize (Zhengdan 958 — proven, stable, I trust it) into the wheat stubble with a no-till planter right after the June wheat harvest. No-till saves me three days of field prep work in the summer heat and retains stubble moisture. I fertilize heavily at sowing and topdress nitrogen at the V6 stage. Summer rainfall in Quzhou covers most of the water demand — I'll irrigate once at VT/R1 (tasseling/silking) if July is dry, and possibly once more at grain fill. Two pesticide applications: one for corn borer (we spray around the 3rd instar), one for fall armyworm which has become a problem in recent years.

I keep 0.3 mu near the house for vegetables — garlic, cabbage, peppers — but that's subsistence, not a commercial plan.
